name: Kerala Mural Painting
tagline: Temple-wall murals in vivid natural pigments and classical iconography
summary: Kerala mural painting is a centuries-old temple and palace wall tradition noted for bold outlines, five core colours and mythic themes; visitors see large narrative panels across temples, palaces and…
description: Kerala mural painting is a classical South Indian wall-painting tradition that decorates temple sanctums, palace halls and some churches with large narrative scenes drawn from Hindu epics, Puranic stories and local legend. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/shopping-options/shop-mural-paintings-kerala/8/?utm_source=openai))

The style grows from medieval Kerala pictorial practice and temple ritual texts; surviving murals reach back many centuries and the tradition is recorded, studied and archived by local and academic projects. ([keralamuralarchive.in](https://keralamuralarchive.in/explore-murals/?utm_source=openai))

Traditional technique uses a multi-layer lime-and-clay plaster ground and natural pigments applied in tempera-like fashion; a limited palette (the classical five colours) and strict iconographic rules produce the flat, rhythmic figures and rich backgrounds. ([escholarship.org](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2r0751tf?utm_source=openai))

Kerala murals are a living craft: revival training centres and contemporary commissions keep the language alive while conservation projects document and stabilise fragile temple paintings. Visitors gain direct contact with devotional imagery, skilled artists and museum displays of the form. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Mural_Painting?utm_source=openai))
highlights: Large narrative panels in temples and palaces with scenes from Ramayana, Mahabharata and Vishnu/Lakshmi cycles
Traditional five-colour palette and lime-plaster ground
Sites with notable murals: Pundareekapuram, Ettumanur, Vadakkunathan, Padmanabhaswamy and Mattancherry
Institutes and workshops teaching traditional methods and conservation
A living tradition with recent public commissions and museum installations

sections.heading: Background
body: Kerala murals develop from temple culture and medieval patronage; stylistically they synthesise regional South Indian pictorial conventions into bold, frontal figures and stylised ornament. Key temple cycles date to the medieval and early modern periods and continue to be important visual records of local religious life. ([keralamuralarchive.in](https://keralamuralarchive.in/explore-murals/?utm_source=openai))

sections.heading: Materials and technique
body: Painters prepare walls with a sequence of coarse mud and a final lime-rich plaster; pigment is traditionally mineral and organic (earth reds, ochres, charcoal, lime-based white and plant-derived greens) and applied in layers to build colour fields and fine linework. The approach is close to tempera on lime plaster rather than true fresco, and the ‘five colours’ are central to the aesthetic. ([escholarship.org](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2r0751tf?utm_source=openai))

Iconography and proportions follow classical shilpa (artisan) texts and temple convention; outlines and ornament are added with fine brushwork and scenes are arranged in horizontal bands or framed panels that fit the temple architecture. ([keralamuralarchive.in](https://keralamuralarchive.in/explore-murals/?utm_source=openai))

sections.heading: Where to see and learn
body: Major places to view authentic temple murals include Pundareekapuram (Kottayam area), Ettumanur and Vaikom (Kottayam/Ettumanoor region), Vadakkunathan (Thrissur), Padmanabhaswamy (Thiruvananthapuram) and the Mattancherry palace and temple precincts in Kochi. Many of these sites are documented in surveys and academic projects. ([sathee.iitk.ac.in](https://sathee.iitk.ac.in/pa/sathee-ssc/student-corner/ncert-books/class-11/an-introduction-to-indian-art/chapter-05-later-mural-traditions/?utm_source=openai))

Training and conservation: the post-restoration era saw formal training centres and institutes focused on mural technique and conservation; look for workshops run by cultural centres and specialist institutes teaching traditional methods. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Mural_Painting?utm_source=openai))

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Allow time at temple sites: murals are best seen in calm daylight and often require permission for close-up photography—ask temple staff or priests. Many murals sit in active ritual spaces; plan around puja schedules and festival days for access. (Confirm times before you travel.)

If you want hands-on learning, check local cultural centres and verified studio workshops for short courses or demonstrations; many run periodic mural painting courses aimed at visitors and artists. ([rkmvcc.org](https://rkmvcc.org/blogs/post/kerala-mural-painting-workshop-%E2%80%93-4th-batch-july-2026?utm_source=openai))

latest.text: Kerala mural artist Basanth Peringode’s mural works are reported installed as a permanent exhibit at the Rashtrapati Bhavan Museum in New Delhi, a national-level recognition for Kerala mural art.
Community and cultural centres ran short Kerala mural painting workshops (4th batch July 2026 reported), reflecting continued demand for practical training.

A public mural project (reported April 11, 2026) used acrylics while preserving classical mural motifs during a recent temple repainting, showing flexibility in materials for contemporary commissions.

visitorInfo.bestTime: October–March (dry, pleasant weather and festival season). ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/faq/20-things-to-know-before-you-visit-kerala?utm_source=openai))
visitorInfo.howToReach: Kerala is served by three major international airports (Kochi/Cochin, Thiruvananthapuram, Kozhikode), an extensive rail network and state bus services; reach major mural sites by road from nearby railway stations or airports. Check local connections for individual temples. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/ktadmin/img/file_upload/lowres/palakkad_final.pdf?utm_source=openai))
etiquette: Temples are active ritual spaces — dress modestly, ask before photographing, and avoid touching painted surfaces.
Check temple opening hours and festival dates in advance; some murals are accessible only outside puja times (confirm before you travel).
Buy authenticated reproductions or work directly from recognised mural studios and training centres to support artisans.
